To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

self-training with deep neural networks can work under a simple and realistic assumption that we call the “expansion” condition, that the expansion condition is sufficient for the minimizer of the input consistency objective to achieve high accuracy, and that the expansion condition can be checked empirically.

self-training algorithms with input consistency regularization can be used to learn with unlabeled data, and the sample complexity of such algorithms scales polynomially in the margin and the Lipschitzness.

self-training with deep neural networks can be theoretically analyzed using a simple expansion assumption, and that our analysis provides sample complexity guarantees that explain the success of self-training with neural nets.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.
the theoretical analysis of self-supervision and unsupervised domain adaption.

the following questions: What is the theoretical justification for self-training with neural networks? What is the theoretical relationship between self-training, input consistency regularization, and other approaches? What is the relationship between self-training and other semi-supervised and unsupervised algorithms?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
self-training algorithms are theoretically justified and can achieve high accuracy in practice, as long as the data is sufficiently structured and the model is sufficiently powerful.
self-training is an effective and robust way of using unlabeled data for learning with neural nets.
the self-training algorithms are not only effective, but also theoretically justified, and the theoretical justification is not only for linear models but also for deep neural networks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we prove that self-training is theoretically justified, but it is not the best algorithm.
we provide the theoretical analysis for why self-training works, and the theoretical justification for the use of consistency regularization in self-training algorithms.

we provide a unified theoretical analysis for self-training algorithms in three scenarios, namely semi-supervised learning (SSL), unsupervised domain adaption (UDA), and unsupervised representation learning (UPL), and our analysis is based on two simple but realistic assumptions.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in contrast to the case of linear models, the performance of self-training with neural networks does not degrade when the data are not linearly separable, as long as they are separable in the neighborhood of the data points.
, in contrast to linear models, self-training and input consistency regularization are complementary and can be used simultaneously to obtain improved performance.
self-training can work well in practice even if the expansion assumption does not hold exactly.
